fetched_contents.title: Spring and Spring Boot Frameworks: A Brief History
fetched_contents.text: Spring and Spring Boot Frameworks: A Brief History Initially launched in 2002, Spring and the various frameworks built on top of it, such as Spring Boot, have come to dominate the way Java developers write code. The developer Rod Johnson came up with the idea of Spring in 2002. The following year, Jonhnson, along with Juergen Hoeller and Yann Caroff, developed Spring as an open source framwork. They created Spring in order to make Java server-side development easier and to allow dev teams to more quickly create their applications. Given that Spring finished as the fourth 'Most Loved Framework' in Stack Overflow's 2019 developer survey, I'd say they succeeded. The Spring Framework: Why it Was Made Prior to Spring, Java developers relied on traditional Java EE to create their applications. As outlined by this excellent Quora post, this led to three main problems: 1. Writing code became more and more complex, as developers had to draw on countless XML files and work with several different types of configurations. 2. Components proved exceeedingly frustrating to work with, as developers had to hard-code all the dependencies each componetent required. 3. All of Java EE's features were supported, and thus needed to be configued. This led to very bloated code that slowed down applications. These were the problems Spring hoped to address. In the book where Rod Johnson originally laid out the programming concepts that led to the Spring framework, he called for greater use of dependency injection and POJOs. Throughout his work, Johnson wrote some 30,000 lines of code to demonstrate how this could work in Java EE. Once his book released, he, Hoeller, and Caroff began working on their own framework that could incorporate these ideas. Thus Spring was born. Originally released under the Apache license as Spring 0.9, developers quickly took up this new framework. By the time Johnson et al released Spring 1.0 the following year, they already had a burgeoning developer community on their hands. In all the releases since, the team of developer's behind the Spring framework have tried to make Spring easier and more fun to work with. To that end, in 2014, the Spring team realeased their next hit, Spring Boot. The Spring Boot Framework In 2012, an issue was filed on the Spring GitHub repo title, "Improved support for 'containerless' web applicaiton architectures." The issue's athor, Mike Youngstrom, wrote that "Traditionally Spring web applications have been embedded in a servlet container. This was useful in the past when the majority of enterprise applications ran in and depended on the servlet container for deployment and configuration. However, a servlet container comes with learning curve that we cannot assume new developers will have already overcome." His solution? Make it easier. "I think that Spring's web application architecture can be significantly simplified," Youngstrom went on, "if it were to provide tools and a reference architecture that leveraged the Spring component and configuration model from top to bottom. Embedding and unifying the configuration of those common web container services within a Spring Container bootstrapped from a simple main() method." If you scroll down a bit on this repo page, you come to Phil Webb's comments. Mr. Webb, it just so happens, was a member of the Spring team. On August 6, 2013, Phil wrote, "Rather than fix this as part of the core Spring Framework we have decided to start a new project called Spring Boot that addresses this and a number of other issues." Phil Webb went on to co-create Spring Boot. So, it seems we can safely say that Spring Boot came about as way to make architecting and developing web applications with Spring more approachable. According to Spring Boot's README on GitHub, it "makes it easy to create Spring-powered, production-grade applications and services with absolute minimum fuss. It takes an opionated view of the Spring platform so that new and existing users can quickly get to the bits they need." Spring Boot's easy to use nature has led to rapid and widespread adoption. According to JetBrains's 2019 Developer Ecosystem survey, 56% of those surveyed said they use the Spring Boot framework when developing web applications, an increase of 14% over their previous year's survey. Additionally, 61% of respondents told JetBrains that they use Spring Boot as an alternative to application servers. Spring Tutorials and Spring Boot Tutorials Now that you know the history of these frameworks are you ready to dive into some code? We've put together some of the best tutorials on DZone about Spring and Spring Boot in a few handy resources. Happy coding! 1. Put a Spring in Your Step: Spring Framework Tutorials 2. fetched_contents.text: Inversion of Control and Dependency Injection with Spring 1. Overview In this tutorial, we’ll introduce the concepts of IoC (Inversion of Control) and DI (Dependency Injection), as well as take a look at how these are implemented in the Spring framework. 2. What Is Inversion of Control? Inversion of Control is a principle in software engineering which transfers the control of objects or portions of a program to a container or framework. We most often use it in the context of object-oriented programming. In contrast with traditional programming, in which our custom code makes calls to a library, IoC enables a framework to take control of the flow of a program and make calls to our custom code. To enable this, frameworks use abstractions with additional behavior built in. If we want to add our own behavior, we need to extend the classes of the framework or plugin our own classes. The advantages of this architecture are: * decoupling the execution of a task from its implementation * making it easier to switch between different implementations * greater modularity of a program * greater ease in testing a program by isolating a component or mocking its dependencies, and allowing components to communicate through contracts We can achieve Inversion of Control through various mechanisms such as: Strategy design pattern, Service Locator pattern, Factory pattern, and Dependency Injection (DI). We’re going to look at DI next. 3. What Is Dependency Injection? Dependency injection is a pattern we can use to implement IoC, where the control being inverted is setting an object’s dependencies. Connecting objects with other objects, or “injecting” objects into other objects, is done by an assembler rather than by the objects themselves. Here’s how we would create an object dependency in traditional programming: public class Store { private Item item; public Store() { item = new ItemImpl1(); } } In the example above, we need to instantiate an implementation of the Item interface within the Store class itself. By using DI, we can rewrite the example without specifying the implementation of the Item that we want: public class Store { private Item item; public Store(Item item) { this.item = item; } } In the next sections, we’ll look at how we can provide the implementation of Item through metadata. Both IoC and DI are simple concepts, but they have deep implications in the way we structure our systems, so they’re well worth understanding fully. 4. The Spring IoC Container An IoC container is a common characteristic of frameworks that implement IoC. In the Spring framework, the interface ApplicationContext represents the IoC container. The Spring container is responsible for instantiating, configuring and assembling objects known as beans, as well as managing their life cycles. The Spring framework provides several implementations of the ApplicationContext interface: AnnotationConfigApplicationContext, ClassPathXmlApplicationContext and FileSystemXmlApplicationContext for standalone applications, and WebApplicationContext for web applications. In order to assemble beans, the container uses configuration metadata, which can be in the form of XML configuration or annotations. Here’s one way to manually instantiate a container: ApplicationContext context = new ClassPathXmlApplicationContext("applicationContext.xml"); And here’s an example of manually instantiating a container using AnnotationConfigApplicationContext: AnnotationConfigApplicationContext annotationContext = new AnnotationConfigApplicationContext(); When you create an instance of AnnotationConfigApplicationContext and provide it with one or more configuration classes, it scans these classes for the @Bean annotations and other relevant annotations. It then initializes and manages the beans defined in these classes, setting up their dependencies and managing their lifecycle. You can find the detailed example here. To set the item attribute in the example above, we can use metadata. Then the container will read this metadata and use it to assemble beans at runtime. Dependency Injection in Spring can be done through constructors, setters or fields. 5. Constructor-Based Dependency Injection In the case of constructor-based dependency injection, the container will invoke a constructor with arguments each representing a dependency we want to set. Spring resolves each argument primarily by type, followed by name of the attribute, and index for disambiguation. Let’s see the configuration of a bean and its dependencies using annotations: @Configuration public class AppConfig { @Bean public Item item1() { return new ItemImpl1(); } @Bean public Store store() { return new Store(item1()); } } The @Configuration annotation indicates that the class is a source of bean definitions. We can also add it to multiple configuration classes. We use the @Bean annotation on a method to define a bean. If we don’t specify a custom name, then the bean name will default to the method name. For a bean with the default singleton scope, Spring first checks if a cached instance of the bean already exists, and only creates a new one if it doesn’t. If we’re using the prototype scope, the container returns a new bean instance for each method call. Another way to create the configuration of the beans is through XML configuration: <bean id="item1" class="org.baeldung.store.ItemImpl1" /> <bean id="store" class="org.baeldung.store.Store"> <constructor-arg type="ItemImpl1" index="0" name="item" ref="item1" /> </bean> 6. It is a process whereby objects define their dependencies (that is, the other objects they work with) only through constructor arguments, arguments to a factory method, or properties that are set on the object instance after it is constructed or returned from a factory method. The container then injects those dependencies when it creates the bean. This process is fundamentally the inverse (hence the name, Inversion of Control) of the bean itself controlling the instantiation or location of its dependencies by using direct construction of classes or a mechanism such as the Service Locator pattern. This can be a useful feature when working in an IDE, as it gives a very fast feedback loop for code changes. By default, any entry on the classpath that points to a directory is monitored for changes. Note that certain resources, such as static assets and view templates, do not need to restart the application. If you are restarting with Maven or Gradle using the build plugin you must leave the forking set to enabled. If you disable forking, the isolated application classloader used by devtools will not be created and restarts will not operate properly. Automatic restart works very well when used with LiveReload. See the LiveReload section for details. If you use JRebel, automatic restarts are disabled in favor of dynamic class reloading. Other devtools features (such as LiveReload and property overrides) can still be used. DevTools relies on the application context’s shutdown hook to close it during a restart. It does not work correctly if you have disabled the shutdown hook (SpringApplication.setRegisterShutdownHook(false)). Automatic restart is not supported when using AspectJ weaving. Logging Changes in Condition Evaluation By default, each time your application restarts, a report showing the condition evaluation delta is logged. The report shows the changes to your application’s auto-configuration as you make changes such as adding or removing beans and setting configuration properties. To disable the logging of the report, set the following property: * Properties * YAML spring.devtools.restart.log-condition-evaluation-delta=false spring: devtools: restart: log-condition-evaluation-delta: false Excluding Resources Certain resources do not necessarily need to trigger a restart when they are changed. For example, Thymeleaf templates can be edited in-place. By default, changing resources in /META-INF/maven, /META-INF/resources, /resources, /static, /public, or /templates does not trigger a restart but does trigger a live reload. If you want to customize these exclusions, you can use the spring.devtools.restart.exclude property. For example, to exclude only /static and /public you would set the following property: * Properties * YAML spring.devtools.restart.exclude=static/**,public/** spring: devtools: restart: exclude: "static/**,public/**" If you want to keep those defaults and add additional exclusions, use the spring.devtools.restart.additional-exclude property instead. Watching Additional Paths You may want your application to be restarted or reloaded when you make changes to files that are not on the classpath. To do so, use the spring.devtools.restart.additional-paths property to configure additional paths to watch for changes. You can use the spring.devtools.restart.exclude property described earlier to control whether changes beneath the additional paths trigger a full restart or a live reload. In most cases, you can set this property in your application.properties (doing so still initializes the restart classloader, but it does not watch for file changes). To do so, you can use a “trigger file”, which is a special file that must be modified when you want to actually trigger a restart check. Any update to the file will trigger a check, but restart only actually occurs if Devtools has detected it has something to do. To use a trigger file, set the spring.devtools.restart.trigger-file property to the name (excluding any path) of your trigger file. The trigger file must appear somewhere on your classpath. Branch report on the problems Servlets and JSP aimed to solve

Servlets and JSP emerged as a direct replacement for CGI (Common Gateway Interface), addressing its major shortcomings. CGI was useful for dynamic web content, but it was inefficient because each request triggered a new process, and developers often had to write standalone scripts in languages like Perl or C for each web page. Servlets solved this by providing a reusable Java-based runtime environment that could handle multiple requests in a single process, making it easier to build dynamic web pages [N1-R1]. The same source also notes that servlets made web development easier, but new problems emerged: mixing business logic and UI in one file made debugging a nightmare [N1-R1]. This shows that servlets aimed to improve performance and reuse while introducing new architectural challenges.

The main limitations of manual servlet and JSP configuration were complexity and boilerplate. Before Spring, Java developers often had to rely on traditional Java EE, which required extensive XML configuration, multiple configuration files, and manual setup of dependencies. The DZone history excerpt states that developers had to work with countless XML files and hard-code dependencies for each component, leading to bloated code that slowed down applications [N1-F1]. This manual setup meant developers spent more time configuring the environment than writing business logic, and the resulting codebase became harder to maintain. The same source also emphasizes that Java EE’s features were supported, but all had to be configured explicitly, which made the application architecture more cumbersome [N1-F1].

Boilerplate and deployment complexity emerged because the manual process required developers to define every piece of the application from scratch. This included not only coding servlets and JSPs but also setting up the servlet container, configuring web descriptors, and managing dependencies manually. The evidence shows that early Spring was created precisely because this approach made code more complex, dependencies harder to manage, and configuration more tedious [N1-F1]. In short, servlets and JSP provided a more efficient and reusable way to build dynamic web pages than CGI, but the manual configuration and deployment burden created a need for a better framework to simplify the development process [N1-R1][N1-F1].

Spring’s core design is built around two central concepts: dependency injection (DI) and inversion of control (IoC). DI is a software design technique in which the creation and binding of dependencies are done outside the dependent class, while IoC is the principle that transfers control of objects or portions of a program to a container or framework [N3-R2][N3-R3]. The Baeldung explanation makes it clear that these are distinct but often combined concepts: DI is a pattern used to implement IoC, where the container sets an object’s dependencies instead of the object itself instantiating them [N3-F2]. This is central to Spring’s architecture because it allows developers to write loosely coupled, modular code that is easier to test and maintain.

Spring simplifies Java EE application configuration by reducing the need for manual XML configuration and hard-coded dependencies. The official Spring core reference explains that the IoC container is responsible for instantiating, configuring, and assembling objects known as beans, and that developers can use XML, Java annotations, or Java code as configuration metadata [N5-F3]. This means instead of manually writing dozens of XML files for every configuration item, developers can use annotations or code-based configuration to define beans and their dependencies. The same source also notes that ApplicationContext adds enterprise-specific functionality to the basic BeanFactory, making it easier to integrate with AOP, message resources, events, and web-specific contexts [N5-F3]. This is a major simplification over traditional Java EE, where developers had to hard-code dependencies and manually configure each component [N1-F1].

Spring’s core modules and developer-facing responsibilities are centered around the IoC container and AOP. The Spring Framework’s core technologies include the IoC container and AOP, with the latter being conceptually easy to understand and addressing the 80% sweet spot of AOP requirements in Java enterprise programming [N5-R1]. The core reference also states that Spring provides its own AOP framework and integrates with AspectJ, which is the richest and most mature AOP implementation in the Java enterprise space [N5-F3]. For developers, this means Spring can manage cross-cutting concerns like logging, transaction management, and security through declarative configuration rather than scattered boilerplate code. The core reference also emphasizes that Spring controls the entire lifecycle of a bean, including creation, initialization, and dependency injection, and that developers use the ApplicationContext interface to manage beans and their relationships [N5-F3]. In short, Spring’s core design gives developers a lightweight, configurable, and modular framework that reduces boilerplate and makes enterprise Java development more maintainable [N3-R2][N3-R3][N5-F3].

# Integrated final answer: evolution from Java Servlets to Spring Boot, problems solved, and Spring essentials

## 1) The historical evolution: from Servlets to Spring Boot

The evolution of Java web development began with Servlets as a replacement for CGI. CGI was useful for dynamic web content, but it was inefficient because each request triggered a new process, and developers often had to write standalone scripts in languages like Perl or C for each web page. Servlets solved this by providing a reusable Java-based runtime environment that could handle multiple requests in a single process, making it easier to build dynamic web pages [N1-R1]. This was a major step forward for Java web development, but it also introduced new problems, including mixing business logic and UI in one file, which made debugging a nightmare [N1-R1].

Over time, manual servlet and JSP development became increasingly complex and error-prone. The branch report on Servlets and JSP explains that developers had to work with countless XML files, hard-code dependencies for each component, and manually configure everything, which led to bloated code that slowed down applications [N1-F1]. This complexity and boilerplate made configuration tedious and deployment difficult. The evidence shows that these problems were serious enough to justify the creation of a new framework that could simplify the process [N1-F1].

## 2) Problems each iteration aimed to solve

### Servlets/JSP: performance and reuse vs. complexity
Servlets provided a more efficient and reusable way to build dynamic web pages than CGI [N1-R1]. But the same source notes that the new problems included mixing business logic and UI in one file, which made debugging hard [N1-R1]. The key issue was that while servlets improved performance and reuse, they did not eliminate the need for manual configuration and deployment complexity [N1-R1][N1-F1].

### Java EE: configuration explosion and dependency management
Before Spring, Java developers relied on traditional Java EE, which required extensive XML configuration, multiple configuration files, and hard-coded dependencies. The branch report states that developers had to work with countless XML files and hard-code dependencies for each component, leading to bloated code and slower applications [N1-F1]. This manual setup meant developers spent more time configuring the environment than writing business logic, and the resulting codebase became harder to maintain [N1-F1].

### Spring: decoupling, configuration simplification, and modular architecture
Spring was created to address these Java EE limitations. The branch report explains that Spring was born because Java EE development had become too complex, dependencies were hard to manage, and configuration was too tedious [N1-F1]. Spring’s solution centered on dependency injection and inversion of control, which decouple components, make dependencies easier to manage, and reduce boilerplate configuration [N3-R2][N3-R3][N5-F3]. This allowed developers to build more modular, testable, and maintainable applications.

### Spring Boot: automation and opinionated defaults
Spring Boot was created to make architecting and developing web applications with Spring more approachable, with the goal of “creating Spring-powered, production-grade applications and services with absolute minimum fuss” [N1-F1]. Its main aim was to eliminate the most tedious parts of Spring development by automating configuration, defaults, and common setup tasks [N1-F1]. This matters because it lets developers focus on application logic rather than boilerplate configuration [N1-F1].

## 3) Core Spring functionalities and developer essentials

### Dependency injection and inversion of control: the foundation
Spring’s core design is built around two central concepts: dependency injection (DI) and inversion of control (IoC). DI is a software design technique in which the creation and binding of dependencies are done outside the dependent class, while IoC is the principle that transfers control of objects or portions of a program to a container or framework [N3-R2][N3-R3]. The branch report explains that DI is a pattern used to implement IoC, where the container sets an object’s dependencies instead of the object itself instantiating them [N3-F2]. This is central to Spring’s architecture because it allows developers to write loosely coupled, modular code that is easier to test and maintain [N3-R2][N3-R3].

### How Spring simplifies Java EE application configuration
Spring simplifies Java EE application configuration by reducing the need for manual XML configuration and hard-coded dependencies. The official Spring core reference explains that the IoC container is responsible for instantiating, configuring, and assembling objects known as beans, and that developers can use XML, Java annotations, or Java code as configuration metadata [N5-F3]. This means instead of manually writing dozens of XML files for every configuration item, developers can use annotations or code-based configuration to define beans and their dependencies [N5-F3]. The same source also notes that ApplicationContext adds enterprise-specific functionality to the basic BeanFactory, making it easier to integrate with AOP, message resources, events, and web-specific contexts [N5-F3]. This is a major simplification over traditional Java EE, where developers had to hard-code dependencies and manually configure each component [N1-F1].

### Core modules and developer-facing responsibilities
The branch report identifies Spring’s core modules as the IoC container and AOP. Spring provides its own AOP framework and integrates with AspectJ, which is the richest and most mature AOP implementation in the Java enterprise space [N5-R1][N5-F3]. For developers, this means Spring can manage cross-cutting concerns like logging, transaction management, and security through declarative configuration rather than scattered boilerplate code [N5-F3]. The core reference also emphasizes that Spring controls the entire lifecycle of a bean, including creation, initialization, and dependency injection, and that developers use the ApplicationContext interface to manage beans and their relationships [N5-F3]. In short, Spring’s core design gives developers a lightweight, configurable, and modular framework that reduces boilerplate and makes enterprise Java development more maintainable [N3-R2][N3-R3][N5-F3].

## 4) Spring Boot’s design and developer workflow

### What Spring Boot automates and why that matters
Spring Boot automates the most tedious parts of Spring development, making it easier to create production-grade applications with minimal setup. Its design philosophy is described as “opinionated,” meaning it makes sensible defaults so developers can get to the bits they need quickly [N1-F1]. This matters because it eliminates the need to manually configure every aspect of the application, including dependencies, server settings, and common configurations [N1-F1]. The branch report states that Spring Boot was created to make architecting and developing web applications with Spring more approachable, with the goal of “creating Spring-powered, production-grade applications and services with absolute minimum fuss” [N1-F1]. This automation is especially valuable in a world where manual configuration had become complex, bloated, and error-prone [N1-F1].

### Key starter projects and autoconfiguration behavior
A key part of Spring Boot’s automation is starter projects and autoconfiguration. Starters are curated bundles of dependencies that simplify project setup. The evidence shows that starter projects bundle complexity so developers can focus on application logic rather than dependency management [N4-R3]. For example, spring-boot-starter-web includes Spring MVC, Embedded Tomcat, Jackson, and Validation API, which together provide a ready-to-use web application stack [N4-R2]. Autoconfiguration behavior is the mechanism by which Spring Boot automatically configures beans based on the declared dependencies in the project. The same source states that autoconfiguration reduces friction by aligning setup with declared dependencies [N4-R3]. This means Spring Boot can infer common configuration settings without requiring developers to write explicit XML or boilerplate Java configuration.

### Essential tools and practices for Spring Boot developers
The branch report emphasizes that Spring Boot includes an additional set of tools that can make the application development experience a little more pleasant [N6-R1]. The developer workflow is also supported by practices such as using starter projects, autoconfiguration, and a modern development workflow that emphasizes rapid iteration. The evidence indicates that developers can quickly create boilerplate configuration with a few mouse clicks or keystrokes in tools like Spring Tools for Eclipse [N1-F1]. More generally, Spring Boot developers should understand how starter projects reduce dependency management, how autoconfiguration aligns with declared dependencies, and how configuration metadata can be expressed through annotations, Java code, or XML [N4-R2][N4-R3][N5-F3]. This workflow makes Spring Boot ideal for developers who want to build applications faster while keeping configuration manageable and maintainable [N4-R2][N4-R3].

## 5) Spring Boot’s ecosystem and deployment tooling

### DevTools, profiles, and configuration management
Spring Boot’s ecosystem and tooling are centered around DevTools, profiles, and configuration management. DevTools is a key addition that makes development faster and more convenient. The official documentation says Spring Boot includes an additional set of tools that can make the application development experience a little more pleasant, and the DevTools section explains that applications using spring-boot-devtools automatically restart whenever files on the classpath change [N6-R1][N6-F4]. This is especially useful in an IDE, where it provides a fast feedback loop for code changes [N6-F4]. DevTools also supports LiveReload, which can trigger a browser refresh when a resource is changed, and it provides property overrides and other features that help developers iterate more efficiently [N6-F4]. However, it is important to note that DevTools is not suitable for production use and should be disabled in production environments, as the same source explains that devtools should be flagged as optional to prevent them from being transitively applied to other modules [N7-R4].

Profiles and configuration management are essential for managing environment-specific settings. Spring Boot profiles allow developers to create different application configurations depending on the environment, such as dev, staging, and production [N6-R4][N7-R2]. The evidence shows that developers can select a profile using the Spring Boot Maven Plugin with `-Drun.profiles` and that Spring Boot profiles manage environment-specific configs with secure, clean, scalable configuration practices [N6-R5][N7-R2]. This means developers can define different data sources, logging levels, external services, and other settings for each environment without duplicating code. The configuration management is also tightly integrated with Spring Boot’s autoconfiguration and starter projects, which reduce the need to manually define every configuration detail [N6-R5][N4-R2].

### Embedded server behavior and deployment flexibility
Embedded server behavior and deployment flexibility are a major part of Spring Boot’s appeal. The evidence states that Spring Boot provides embedded servers so that no WAR deployment is required [N7-R5]. This means developers can package applications as standalone JARs and run them directly without deploying to an external servlet container, which greatly simplifies deployment. The embedded server behavior also aligns with Spring Boot’s opinionated design: it makes it easier to run, test, and deploy applications with minimal setup [N7-R5]. In practice, this gives developers flexibility to choose between embedded servers such as Tomcat, Jetty, or Undertow, and to deploy the same application in different environments without rewriting the configuration [N7-R5].

### Practical deployment and runtime practices
Practical deployment and runtime practices include disabling DevTools in production, customizing restart behavior, and using profiles effectively. The evidence advises disabling DevTools for production by setting `spring.devtools.restart.enabled=false`, either in `application.properties` or as a system property before calling `SpringApplication.run()` [N6-F4]. It also explains how to customize restart exclusions and additional paths, and how to use a trigger file to control when restarts occur [N6-F4]. For runtime practices, Spring Boot’s configuration management and profiles are the core mechanisms for separating dev, test, and prod settings, while the embedded server and autoconfiguration make deployment simpler and more consistent across environments [N6-R5][N7-R2][N7-R5]. Overall, Spring Boot’s ecosystem and tooling are designed to shorten the feedback loop during development and make runtime and deployment more predictable and maintainable [N6-F4][N7-R2][N7-R5].

## 6) Essential knowledge for developers working with Spring

If you’re working with Spring, the essential knowledge includes:

- **Dependency injection and inversion of control**: Understand how Spring manages dependencies and controls object creation, which is the foundation of modular and testable code [N3-R2][N3-R3][N3-F2].
- **Beans and configuration metadata**: Know that Spring uses beans and configuration metadata to assemble applications, and that metadata can come from XML, annotations, or code [N5-F3].
- **ApplicationContext and BeanFactory**: Understand the difference between the basic BeanFactory and the more feature-rich ApplicationContext, and how they manage bean lifecycles [N5-F3].
- **AOP**: Be familiar with Spring’s Aspect-Oriented Programming support, including how it can manage cross-cutting concerns like logging, transaction management, and security [N5-R1][N5-F3].
- **Autoconfiguration and starters**: Know how Spring Boot uses autoconfiguration and starter projects to reduce boilerplate and align setup with dependencies [N4-R2][N4-R3].
- **Profiles and configuration management**: Understand how profiles let you manage environment-specific settings cleanly and securely [N6-R4][N7-R2].
- **DevTools and embedded servers**: Know when to use DevTools during development and how embedded servers simplify deployment [N6-R1][N6-F4][N7-R5].

## 7) Synthesis: evolution, problems, and essentials in one view

The evolution from Java Servlets to Spring Boot is the story of a series of improvements driven by concrete problems. Servlets replaced CGI with a reusable Java runtime, but they introduced complexity and boilerplate. Java EE made things even worse by requiring manual XML configuration and hard-coded dependencies [N1-R1][N1-F1]. Spring solved those problems by introducing dependency injection and inversion of control, reducing boilerplate, and simplifying configuration [N3-R2][N3-R3][N5-F3]. Spring Boot then built on that by automating configuration, defaults, and common setup tasks, making it easier to create production-grade applications with minimal fuss [N1-F1].

For developers, the essentials are: understand Spring’s DI and IoC model, master beans and configuration metadata, know how AOP works, and be comfortable with autoconfiguration and starter projects. In Spring Boot, you also need to understand profiles, configuration management, and DevTools, along with the embedded server behavior that makes deployment simpler [N3-R2][N3-R3][N5-F3][N4-R2][N4-R3][N6-R4][N7-R5].

In short, the journey from Servlets to Spring Boot reflects a continuous effort to make Java web development faster, simpler, and more maintainable, while the Spring ecosystem provides the foundational tools and patterns that make that possible [N1-R1][N1-F1][N3-R2][N5-F3][N4-R2][N6-R1][N7-R5].
